Design Principle 1: Regularity supports simplicity (mnemonics, source operand -> dest operand)
Design Principle 2: Make the common case fast:
Fast common cases (large instructions are pieced into smaller -> minimize hardware complexity, less overhead for common instructions)
Design Principle 3: Smaller is faster. (Few registers, 32 registers as register set)
Design Principle 4: Good design demands good compromises (RISC-V 32-bit encoding, variable-length instruction add complexity, simplicity would also encourage single-instruction format but too restrictive -> 4 main instruction formats, some regularity + simpler decoder hardware, walso accommodating different instruction needs)

Complex Instruction Set Computers (CISC)
- Many special purpose instructions.
- Example: x86. Now almost 900 instructions.
- Typically various encoding lengths (x86, 1-15 bytes)
- Different number of clock cycles, depending on
instruction.
- Overhead on common cases

Reduced Instruction Set Computers (RISC)
- Few, regular instructions. Minimize hardware complexity.
- RISC-V is a good example (ARM mostly RISC)
- Typically fixed instruction lengths (e.g., 4 bytes for RISC-V)
- Typically one clock cycle per instruction (excluding memory
accesses and cache misses)
- Fast common cases (large instructions are pieced into smaller -> minimize hardware complexity, less overhead for common instructions)

RISC-V is the focus because
i) it is relatively easy to understand
ii) many text-books on RISC-V,
iii) A lot of research and focus on it

Name: C to asm
General structure:
1. C-code, a=b+c
The compiler maps (if possible) C variables to registers (a->s_0, b->s_1, c->s_2)
2. RISC-V Assembly Code, add s0, s1, s2
The assembly code is a human-readable form of the machine code
3. RISC-V Machine Code, 0x01248433
Each assembly instruction is mapped to one or more machine code instructions.
In RISC-V, most instructions are 32 bits (there is support for compressed instructions, but we will not tackle them in the course).

Name: Machine code/Instruction format
General structure:
Where a RISC-V program is stored is dictated by a linker (during compilation). In DTEK-V board, we start code immediately at address 0x0.
In RISC-V, each instruction requires exactly one word (32 bits) of space.
RISC-V code must be word-aligned (start at addresses 0,4, 8, C etc.). X86 does not require word alignment.

R-type (register-type), instructions have three register operands: two sources and one destination
(funct7, 7), (rs2, 5), (rs1, 5), (funct3, 3), (rd, 5), (opcode, 7)
Description/Operation:
funct3/7: determines the specific R-type operation to perform.
rs1, rs2: source operands 1 and 2
rd: destination op (where is the result saved)

Description/Operation: Since funct3 for srli and srai is the same (101_2), imm11:5 encodes whether its an arithmetic or logical shift.

Conditional branches compute their addresses relative to the program counter (PC) because the instructions have not enough address bits. Calculate branch target address (BTA): BTA = PC + signext(concat(imm_(12:1),'0'))

Imm: 20-bit immediate value, large, signed-extended
rd: destination operand (where the result should is saved)

rd: destination operand (where the result should is saved), e.g. return address of jal
Imm needs to be concatenated to form the immediate value, The JAL instruction also uses the PC-relative addressing but the immediate is 20 bits

The target address is called JTA instead of BTA and it is computed as:
JTA = PC+signext(concat(imm20:1, ”0”))
Since the imm-field is 20-bits (with an implicit imm_0), we can jump +/- 2MiB.

Note: The jump register (jr 16(rs1)) does not use PC-relative addressing. It jumps to the memory address contained in register rs1 where the least significant bit is overwritten to '0'. The jr instruction is a pseudoinstruction based on jalr, which jumps to the address pointed by the register plus a given sign-extended immediate value.

.globl main        # make the main label global
.equ N, 5          # N = 5
.data              # global data segment
A: .word 5, 42, -88, 2, -5033, 720, 314
str1: .string "RISC-V"
.align 2           # align next data on 2^2-byte boundary
B: .word 0x32A
.bss               # bss segment - variables initialized to 0
C: .space 4
D: .space 1
.balign 4          # align next instruction on 4-byte boundary
.text              # text segment (code)
main:
    la t0, A       # t0 = address of A              = 0x2150
    la t1, str1    # t1 = address of str1           = 0x216C
    la t2, B       # t2 = address of B              = 0x2174
    la t3, C       # t3 = address of C              = 0x2188
    la t4, D       # t4 = address of D              = 0x218C
    lw t5, N*4(t0) # t5 = A[N] = A[5] = 720        = 0x2D0
    lw t6, 0(t2)   # t6 = B = 810                  = 0x32A
    add t5, t5, t6 # t5 = A[N] + C = 720 + 810 = 1530 = 0x5FA
    sw t5, 0(t3)   # C = 1530                      = 0x5FA
    lb t5, N-1(t1) # t5 = str1[N-1] = str1[4] = '-' = 0x2D
    sb t5, 0(t4)   # D = str1[N-1]                 = 0x2D
    la t5, str2    # t5 = address of str2          = 0x140
    lb t6, 8(t5)   # t6 = str2[8] = 'r'            = 0x72
    sb t6, 0(t1)   # str1[0] = 'r'                 = 0x72
    jr ra
.section .rodata
str2: .string "Hello world!"
.end               # end of assembly file

General structure:
Has many more data locations than registers, Accessing memory is slower than accessing registers.
A processor’s word size is the data width it can handle in one operation. A 32-bit processor has 32-bit words. A 64-bit processor has 64-bit words.

The choice of endianness is arbitrary, but creates problems when communicating between processors with different endianness.
- Big-endian: the most significant byte (MSB) of the word is stored at the lowest memory address.
- Little-endian: the least significant byte (LSB) is stored at the lowest memory address.

Name: Stack-based call
General structure:
int diffofsums(int f, int g, int h, int i){
  int result;
  result = (f + g) - (h + i);
  return result;
}

$s3 = result
diffofsums:
    addi sp, sp, -12 <- Make space on stack (stack space, stack frame)
    sw s3, 8(sp) <- Store the registers that will be modified
    sw t0, 4(sp)
    sw t1, 0(sp)
    add t0, a0, a1 <- Execution
    add t1, a2, a3
    sub s3, t0, t1
    add a0, s3, zero
    lw s3, 8(sp) <- Restore
    lw t0, 4(sp)
    lw t1, 0(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 12 <- Deallocate stack
    jr ra <- Return

Name: Preserved and non-preserved
General structure:
Preserved (callee-saved) registers needs to be stack-pushed (s0-s11, ra, sp -> stack above the stack pointer)
Non-preserved (caller-saved): t0-t6, a0-a7-> stack below the stack pointer

# s3 = result
diffofsums:
    addi sp, sp, -4
    sw s3, 0(sp) <- Only s3 needed, save preserved registers
    add t0, a0, a1
    add t1, a2, a3
    sub s3, t0, t1
    add a0, s3, zero
    lw s3, 0(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 4
    jr ra

# a0 = a, a1 = b, s4 = i, s5 = x
f1:
    addi sp, sp, −12    # make room on stack for 3 registers
    sw ra, 8(sp)        # save preserved registers used by f1
    sw s4, −4(sp)
    sw s5, 0(sp)
    add s5, a0, a1      # x = (a + b)
    sub t3, a0, a1      # temp = (a − b)
    mul s5, s5, t3      # x = x * temp = (a + b) * (a − b)
    addi s4, zero, 0    # i = 0
for:
    bge s4, a0, return  # if i >= a, exit loop
    addi sp, sp, −8     # make room on stack for 2 registers
    sw a0, 4(sp)        # save nonpreserved regs. on stack
    sw a1, 0(sp)
    add a0, a1, s4      # argument is b + i
    jal f2              # call f2(b + i)
    add s5, s5, a0      # x = x + f2(b + i)
    lw a0, 4(sp)        # restore nonpreserved registers
    lw a1, 0(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 8
    addi s4, s4, 1      # i++
    j for               # continue for loop
return:
    add a0, zero, s5    # return value is x
    lw ra, 8(sp)        # restore preserved registers
    lw s4, 4(sp)
    lw s5, 0(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 12     # restore sp
    jr ra               # return from f1

# a0 = p,   s4 = r
f2:
    addi sp, sp, −4     # save preserved regs. used by f2
    sw s4, 0(sp)
    addi s4, a0, 5      # r = p + 5
    add a0, s4, a0      # return value is r + p
    lw s4, 0(sp)        # restore preserved registers
    addi sp, sp, 4      # restore sp
    jr ra               # return from f2

Name: Recursive functions (Both preserved and non-preserved are saved and restored)
General structure:
factorial:
    addi sp, sp, -8 <- Push a0, ra
    sw a0, 4(sp)
    sw ra, 0(sp)
    addi t0, zero, 1
    bgt a0, t0, else <- if n > 1 (=t1) -> else
    addi sp, sp, 8 <- Pop+discard a0, ra
    jr ra
else:
    addi a0, a0, -1 <- n = n - 1
    jal factorial <- Recursive call
    lw t1, 4(sp) <- Pop, original n into t1
    lw ra, 0(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 8
    mul a0, t1, a0 <- a0 = n * factorial(n-1), original n
    jr ra
